interactive.title: One curve, three jobs
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on three jobs that share one curve. A label at the top names the job: Ball, Supply or Beam. Each job shows the thing itself above a graph against its input. The graph draws the job's straight-line part as a straight line and its squared part as a curve that climbs ever faster, and marks the gap between them at the slider; the same gap is drawn up from the axis as an upside-down U, the parabola, with its two roots and its peak marked, and readouts for the two parts and the gap. Ball: a ball thrown straight up at 19.6 m/s, an example speed, with a time slider from 0 to 4 s in steps of 0.1 s, opening at 1 s; the time axis runs on a little past 4 s, showing only the two parts there, so their crossing sits inside the graph. The straight-line part, 19.6t metres, is how high it would be after t seconds with no gravity. The squared part, 4.9t² metres, is how far gravity has pulled it below that, 4.9 being half of gravity's roughly 9.8 m/s². The height h = 19.6t − 4.9t² is the gap: at 1 s, 19.6 − 4.9 = 14.7 m. Supply: a 12 V battery with 0.5 Ω inside it, example figures, feeding a load, with a current dial from 0 to 24 A in steps of 1 A, opening at 4 A. The straight-line part, EI = 12I watts, is the power the battery makes, E being its voltage with nothing connected and I the current. The squared part, I²r = 0.5I² watts, is the power its internal resistance r burns, because r drops I × r volts while passing I amps. The load's power P = 12I − 0.5I² is the gap: at 4 A, 48 − 8 = 40 W. Beam: a 6 m beam resting on two simple supports, which let it turn, and carrying 2 kN on every metre, example figures, with a point you drag along it from 0 to 6 m in steps of 0.5 m, opening at 1 m. The load is spread evenly, so each support holds half the 12 kN, 6 kN. The straight-line part, 6x kN·m, is the turning effect about the point of that 6 kN push from the left support, x metres away. The squared part, x² kN·m, is the turning effect the other way of the 2x kN of load on those x metres, which acts as if at their middle, x ÷ 2 from the point: 2x × x ÷ 2. The bending moment M = 6x − x² is the gap: at 1 m, 6 − 1 = 5 kN·m. Screens: 1 opens on Ball and lets you drag the time slider; 2 asks when the ball lands; 3 lights the roots, 0 s and 4 s, where 19.6t = 4.9t², which is 4.9t(4 − t) = 0, and the peak halfway, at 2 s, 39.2 − 19.6 = 19.6 m (the same digits as the launch speed only because of the speed chosen); 4 shows a ball thrown up at 4.9 m/s from a deck 9.8 m above the water, h = 9.8 + 4.9t − 4.9t², whose straight-line part starts at 9.8, with the rule drawn dashed before 0 s, and asks when it hits the water: 9.8 + 4.9t = 4.9t² is t² − t − 2 = 0, (t − 2)(t + 1) = 0, so 2 s or −1 s, and −1 s is before the throw; 5 switches to Supply and lets you turn the dial, lighting the roots 0 A, nothing connected, and 24 A, a short circuit, E ÷ r = 12 ÷ 0.5; 6 asks what current gives the load the most power; 7 lights the peak halfway, 12 A, 144 − 72 = 72 W, with the load's voltage 12 − 0.5 × 12 = 6 V and its resistance 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 Ω, equal to r, and a bar splitting the battery's 144 W into 72 W in the load and 72 W inside; 8 asks what happens to the load's power when its resistance is doubled from 0.5 Ω to 1 Ω: the load and r are in series, 0.5 + 1 = 1.5 Ω in all, so the current becomes 12 ÷ 1.5 = 8 A and the power 8² × 1 = 64 W, which is 64 W of the 12 × 8 = 96 W the battery now makes, about two-thirds rather than half: less power, but less lost; 9 switches to Beam and lets you drag the point, with the turning effects taken about the point and only what lies to its left counted, lighting the roots at the two supports, 0 m and 6 m, where 6x = x²; 10 asks how big the largest bending moment is: at 3 m, 18 − 9 = 9 kN·m, matching wL²/8 = 2 × 6² ÷ 8; 11 is a spot the slip: a worked answer for the deck ball's top in three lines, where line 2 goes halfway from 0 to 2 s and line 3 gets 1 s, and you pick the line that slips, line 2, since the top is halfway between the roots −1 s and 2 s, at 0.5 s; 12 asks the best current and its power for a 24 V supply with 1.5 Ω inside, P = 24I − 1.5I², roots 0 A and 16 A, peak at 8 A, 192 − 96 = 96 W; 13 asks the largest bending moment of a 4 m beam carrying 3 kN on every metre, M = 6x − 1.5x², roots 0 and 4 m, peak at 2 m, 12 − 6 = 6 kN·m. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to pick one answer from three. A wrong pick puts its numbers back into the rule and shows where it fails: on 2, 2 s is the peak and 0.25 s divides the wrong way; on 4, −1 s is before the throw; on 6, 24 A gives the load nothing (288 − 288 = 0 W) and 6 A gives 72 − 18 = 54 W; on 8, 144 W assumes the current stays at 12 A, which would give the load all the 12 × 12 = 144 W the battery makes there; on 10, 18 kN·m leaves out the squared part and 27 kN·m takes one support to hold all 12 kN; on 11, line 1 is right, since both 2 s and −1 s make the rule zero, and line 3 adds up, but at 1 s the ball is back at deck height, 9.8 m; on 12, 192 W leaves out the squared part and 16 A is the short circuit, where all 384 W is lost inside; on 13, 12 kN·m leaves out the squared part and 9 kN·m forgets to square the 2, 6 × 2 − 1.5 × 2 = 9. In every job the roots are where the straight-line part and the squared part are equal, and the peak sits halfway between them because a parabola is the same either side of its line of symmetry.
interactive.ignores: The ball moves straight up and down, and the air's drag is left out. A ball thrown at an angle needs its launch split into an up part and an across part, which takes sine and cosine, in Trigonometry. 9.8 m/s² is a rounded value, and gravity differs slightly from place to place. The dashed curve before 0 s on screen 4 is the rule carried backwards, not the ball. The battery's E and r are held fixed, though a real battery's change with its charge, temperature and age, and the wires' resistance is left out. The beam rests on two simple supports that let it turn, carries only the even load, and its own weight is counted as part of that load; a load at a single point gives straight-line pieces, not a parabola. The picture shows the bending moment, not how far the beam sags, which follows a different rule. The sliders move in steps so the readouts land on readable numbers, shown to two decimal places.

explain.text:
A thrown ball's height, the power a battery gives a load and the bending moment in a beam on two supports carrying an even load all follow one pattern: a straight-line part minus a squared part. That difference is a quadratic, so its graph is an upside-down U. It is zero where the two parts are equal, and highest halfway between those two roots.

Take a ball thrown straight up at 19.6 m/s, an example speed. With no gravity it would rise in step with time, 19.6t metres after t seconds. That is the straight-line part. Gravity adds about 9.8 m/s of downward speed every second, so after t seconds it has added 9.8t. Its average downward speed over that time is halfway from 0 to 9.8t, which is 4.9t, and 4.9t for t seconds pulls the ball 4.9t² metres below the line. That 4.9 is half of gravity's roughly 9.8 m/s².[^1] The fall is squared because two things grow with time together, the downward speed and the time it has had to act. So h = 19.6t − 4.9t². Now say a 12 V battery has 0.5 Ω inside it, example figures. Its voltage with nothing connected, E = 12 V, drives a current I and makes EI = 12I watts, the straight-line part. Its internal resistance r drops I × r volts while passing I amps, so it burns I²r = 0.5I² watts inside, the I²R heat of lesson 6. The load gets what is left, P = 12I − 0.5I², and again two things grow together, the current and the volts it loses inside. A beam's [[bending moment]] at a point is the turning effect, force times distance, of all the forces on one side of it,[^8] which tries to bend the beam there. It is measured in newton metres, like a torque setting, here in kilonewton metres, kN·m. Say a 6 m beam rests on two simple supports, which let it turn, and carries 2 kN on every metre, 12 kN in all. The load is spread evenly, so each support pushes up half of it, 6 kN. At a point x metres from the left support, that push turns with a lever arm of x, giving 6x kN·m. The 2x kN of load on those x metres acts as if at their middle,[^9] x ÷ 2 away, and turns the other way with 2x × x ÷ 2 = x² kN·m. So M = 6x − x², with the load and its lever arm both growing with x.

The roots are where the two parts are equal, so the gap is zero. 19.6t = 4.9t² at 0 s, the throw, and 4 s, the landing. 12I = 0.5I² at 0 A, nothing connected, and 24 A, a short circuit, E ÷ r.[^3] 6x = x² at 0 m and 6 m, the two simple supports, where the bending moment must be zero.[^4] A parabola is the same either side of its line of symmetry, so its peak sits in the middle of its roots:[^5] 19.6 m at 2 s, 72 W at 12 A, and 9 kN·m at 3 m. That 9 kN·m matches wL²/8 at midspan,[^2] with w the load on each metre and L the span: 2 × 6² ÷ 8 = 9. The middle of the roots is also why the battery's best current is exactly half its short-circuit current, E ÷ 2r:[^6] the peak sits halfway between 0 and E ÷ r. At 12 A the load has 12 − 0.5 × 12 = 6 V across it, so its resistance is 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 Ω, the same as r, which is the condition for the most power to reach the load,[^6] called [[maximum power transfer]].

Read every root and peak in its job's terms. A ball thrown up at 4.9 m/s from a deck 9.8 m above the water has h = 9.8 + 4.9t − 4.9t², zero at 2 s and at −1 s. A negative time is before the throw, so you discard it,[^7] and the ball hits the water at 2 s. The load's power is a parabola in the current, not in the load's resistance: P = I²R grows in step with R only while the current stays the same. Double this load to 1 Ω, in series with the battery's 0.5 Ω, and the current falls to 12 ÷ (0.5 + 1) = 8 A, so the power falls to 8² × 1 = 64 W. And the most power is not the most efficient: at 12 A the battery's own 0.5 Ω burns 72 W too, so only half of the 144 W it makes reaches the load. At 1 Ω the battery makes 12 × 8 = 96 W and the load gets 64 W of it, about two-thirds: less power, but less lost. Each job here is a teaching model, the ball without air, the battery with E and r fixed and the beam with only an even load, so real curves differ from these most where those effects are large, and a ball thrown at an angle needs Trigonometry. **Take a squared part from a straight-line part and you get an upside-down U, zero where the two parts are equal and, when it has two such roots, highest halfway between them.**[^5]

analogy.text: Remember the deck hatch with 10 m of seal round its edge? One long side plus one short side is half the seal, 5 m. Make one side x metres and the other is 5 − x, so the opening is x(5 − x) = 5x − x², a straight-line part minus a squared part. It is zero at x = 0 and x = 5 m, where the hatch has no width, and largest halfway, a 2.5 m square of 6.25 m², a little more than the 2 m by 3 m hatch's 6 m².
analogy.breaks: The hatch's two roots are both shapes you can get close to, a hatch ever thinner, while the deck ball's root at −1 s describes nothing and is thrown away. And at the hatch's peak nothing is lost, while at the battery's peak half the power it makes heats the battery itself.

practice.text:
- Work out a battery's short-circuit current on paper, never by shorting its terminals: the current can be large enough to burn wiring or damage the battery.
- Name the input (time, current, distance along) and write the straight-line part and the squared part, each in the job's units.
- Set the two parts equal and solve: take the input out as a common factor, or use the formula from lesson 5.
- Keep only the roots the job can have. A time before the start is thrown away.
- The peak is halfway between the rule's two roots, even when one of them is thrown away. Put that input back into the rule for its size, and say it in the job's units.
- Check the peak another way: x = −b ÷ 2a, or, with the derivative from Calculus fundamentals, where the rule's slope is zero.

**Rule of thumb:** For a battery, maximum power transfer comes at half the short-circuit current, E ÷ 2r, when the load's resistance equals r.[^6] For a beam on two simple supports, which let it turn, with an even load, the largest bending moment is wL²/8, at midspan.[^2]

**Worked example:** Say a beam rests on two simple supports 8 m apart and carries 1.5 kN on every metre. The whole load is 12 kN, so each support pushes up 6 kN. At x metres from one support, M = 6x − 1.5x × x ÷ 2 = 6x − 0.75x². It is zero where 6x = 0.75x², at 0 m and 8 m, the supports. Halfway is 4 m, where M = 24 − 12 = 12 kN·m. Check: wL²/8 = 1.5 × 64 ÷ 8 = 12 kN·m.

**Common mistakes**
- Keeping a root the job cannot have, such as a negative time.
- Putting the peak halfway between the start and the end when they are at different heights. The deck ball peaks at 0.5 s, halfway between its roots −1 s and 2 s, not at 1 s.
- Leaving out the squared part. A 24 V battery with 1.5 Ω inside makes 192 W at 8 A, but the load gets 192 − 96 = 96 W.
- Expecting P = I²R to grow with R when the current changes too. Doubling the load from 0.5 Ω to 1 Ω on the 12 V battery takes it from 72 W to 64 W.
- Taking the most power to the load as the most efficient. At the peak, half the power the battery makes is lost inside it.

interactive.title: One curve, three jobs
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the gap between each job's straight-line part and its squared part closing to zero where they are equal and widest halfway between, when you move that job's slider.

checks.label: The coefficient 4.9 comes from ½ × 9.8, since gravity accelerates objects at approximately 9.8 m/s²: on both ball screens the squared part is 4.9t², and at every time on the slider the ball, its two parts and the gap drawn follow h = 19.6t − 4.9t² (14.7 m at 1 s), to the centimetre shown

The maximum height in a parabola sits in the middle of its roots: on every job the top drawn is halfway between the two roots drawn, where the straight-line part and the squared part are equal, and no setting gives a bigger gap

The output power is a concave parabola in the current, vanishing at the no-load point (I = 0) and the short-circuit point (I = E ÷ r): for both supplies the load gets 0 W at 0 A and at E ÷ r, 24 A and 16 A, more than 0 W between, and each step up in current adds less than the one before

The most power reaches the load when its resistance is exactly the internal resistance r, at the optimal current E ÷ (2r): 12 ÷ (2 × 0.5) = 12 A, where the load has 12 − 0.5 × 12 = 6 V across it and 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 Ω, and 24 ÷ (2 × 1.5) = 8 A; doubling the load to 1 Ω gives 8 A and only 64 W

From a uniformly distributed load w the maximum bending moment is M = w·L²/8, and the peak lands at midspan: 2 × 6² ÷ 8 = 9 kN·m at 3 m and 3 × 4² ÷ 8 = 6 kN·m at 2 m, the largest M drawn on each beam

The bending moment must vanish at the ends of the beam, since there they are simply supported: on both beams M is zero at each support, the roots drawn sit on the supports, and the beam is drawn resting on a support at each end

The negative value of time implies an event before the start of motion, so we discard it: the deck rule has a negative root, drawn dashed before the throw, and it is never accepted as when the ball hits the water

The lesson's numbers follow from the rules: 19.6, 4.9 and 14.7 m at 1 s; 39.2 − 19.6 = 19.6 m at 2 s; 48 − 8 = 40 W at 4 A; 144 − 72 = 72 W at 12 A; 6 − 1 = 5 kN·m at 1 m; 18 − 9 = 9 kN·m at 3 m; the deck ball's roots 2 s and −1 s and top at 0.5 s; 96 W at 8 A on the 24 V supply; 6 kN·m at 2 m on the 4 m beam; and the wrong picks' 4.59 m, 0 W at 24 A, 54 W at 6 A, 27 kN·m and 9 kN·m

Every puzzle accepts only its right answer; before Check its picture shows no answer (no curve it asks about, no answer mark and no answer working); after a right answer the curve and its marks arrive where the rule puts them; and every wrong pick is ringed in red where its own numbers put it, with a red line of working

Every line of working on every screen adds up (each a − b = c, a × b = c and a ÷ b = c in it is true), and at every setting of the time, the current and the point the rows show the rule's own two parts and their gap, with the amber gap between the parts drawn the same length as the amber gap stood up from the axis
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: The opening says the bending moment of any beam carrying an even load peaks halfway between two zeros, but a cantilever (fixed at one end) has no such peak; the pattern holds for a beam resting on two supports, as the example then uses.

wL²/8 at midspan holds for simple supports, as the cited quote says, not for any two supports: a beam built in at both ends has its largest moment, wL²/12, at the ends; the worked example also assumes simple supports.
